title: Biome 2.0 Formatter vs Prettier in 2026: Migration Gotchas, Rule Gaps, and Whether It Is Finally Ready for Production
summary: Biome 2.0 Formatter vs Prettier in 2026: Migration Gotchas, Rule Gaps, and Whether It Is Finally Ready for Production This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review. Biome 2.0 replaces Prettier and ESLint with a single Rust-powered formatter and linter, but the migration exposes formatting edge cases that break diffs, missing rule coverage for React and accessibility plugins, and configuration translation pitfalls that stall teams mid-sprint. Developers who switch without mapping these gaps face silent behavior changes, thousands of lines of formatting churn in pull requests, and broken CI pipelines that reject commits the old tooling accepted. A migration starts, hits formatting drift, and fails with broken diffs and CI rejections The correct approach maps the differences before the migration starts, documents the missing plugins, and stages the rollout to isolate formatting changes from functional commits. A migration maps gaps first, stages formatting changes, and completes cleanly Key Takeaways Biome 2.0 replaces Prettier's formatter and a subset of ESLint's rules, but React-specific linting (like eslint-plugin-react ) and accessibility checks (like eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y ) remain gaps as of late 2026. Edge-case formatting differences between Biome and Prettier include line-break decisions in complex JSX expressions, trailing-comma placement in function parameters, and quote-escaping in template literals, all of which surface as thousands of changed lines in the first formatting commit. Configuration translation from .prettierrc and .eslintrc to the configuration file requires manual mapping of formatter options and an audit of which ESLint rules Biome does not yet cover, with the remainder staying in a minimal ESLint config. Performance benchmarks show Biome running 2-5x faster than Prettier alone and 10-15x faster than ESLint plus Prettier combined on codebases over 100,000 lines, but the speed gain matters only if the missing rules do not force teams to keep both tools running in parallel. Production readiness depends on the project: greenfield TypeScript projects with no React-specific linting needs are safe to migrate immediately, while existing React codebases require a dual-tool setup (Biome for formatting and core linting, ESLint for the React-specific rules) until Biome's plugin ecosystem catches up. What Biome 2.0 Actually Replaces (And What It Does Not) Biome 2.0 is a formatter and a linter, not a complete ESLint replacement. The formatter matches Prettier's output on 95% of real-world code according to the Biome documentation , but the remaining 5% consists of edge cases that produce different line breaks, indentation, or quote usage. The linter covers the core JavaScript and TypeScript rules (unused variables, missing return types, dangerous equality checks) but omits the ecosystem-specific rules that ESLint plugins provide. What Biome replaces: Prettier's formatter for JavaScript, TypeScript, JSX, and JSON ESLint's core rules for syntax errors, unused bindings, and code smells Import sorting (Biome includes a built-in import organizer) What Biome does not replace as of version 2.0: React-specific rules from eslint-plugin-react (prop types, hooks rules, JSX accessibility) Accessibility checks from eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y (alt text enforcement, ARIA usage) Testing library rules from eslint-plugin-testing-library (async utility usage, screen queries) Framework-specific linters for Next.js, Vue, or Angular The gap means teams migrating from a full ESLint setup will keep a minimal .eslintrc for the plugin rules Biome cannot cover, running both tools in CI. Biome covers formatting and core linting but not React-specific or accessibility plugins Formatting Differences Between Biome and Prettier: The Edge Cases That Break Your Diffs The migration from Prettier to Biome produces a formatting commit that touches thousands of lines because the two tools handle edge cases differently. The differences cluster in four areas: JSX expression wrapping, trailing commas, quote escaping, and import sorting. JSX Expression Line Breaks Prettier wraps long JSX expressions at the opening brace when the expression exceeds the print width. Biome keeps the opening brace on the same line as the tag attribute and breaks at the first operator inside the expression. Prettier output: < Component disabled = { user . role !== "admin" && user . permissions . length === 0 } /> Biome output: < Component disabled = { user . role !== "admin" && user . permissions . length === 0 } /> The difference surfaces in every JSX file with complex boolean expressions. Trailing Commas in Function Parameters Prettier adds trailing commas to multi-line function parameters when the target is ES5 or higher. Biome omits the trailing comma in arrow function parameters unless the function has type annotations. Prettier output: const handler = ( event : Event , context : Context , ) => { // ... } ; Biome output: const handler = ( event : Event , context : Context ) => { // ... } ; Quote Escaping in Template Literals Prettier escapes quotes inside template literals when the string contains both single and double quotes. Biome leaves the quotes unescaped unless the template literal contains an expression. Prettier output: const message = `Error: "value" can't be null` ; Biome output: const message = `Error: "value" can't be null` ; The difference appears identical in this example because Biome matches Prettier's default, but in strings with mixed quotes and expressions, Biome escapes differently. Import Sorting Order Biome sorts imports alphabetically within three groups: external dependencies, internal modules, and relative imports. Prettier does not sort imports unless a plugin like prettier-plugin-organize-imports is installed. Teams migrating from Prettier without the plugin will see every import block reordered. Formatter JSX line break Trailing comma Quote escaping Import sorting Prettier At opening brace Always in ES5+ Escapes mixed quotes Plugin-dependent Biome At first operator Omits unless typed Escapes in expressions Built-in alphabetical The migration strategy isolates the formatting commit in a separate pull request with a title like "chore: migrate to Biome formatter" and no functional changes. Reviewers skip the diff and verify the build still passes. A migration run exposes formatting drift, isolates changes in a formatting PR, and merges cleanly Migration Gotchas: Configuration Translation, Git History, and CI Pipeline Changes The migration from Prettier and ESLint to Biome requires translating configuration files, updating pre-commit hooks, and changing CI commands, all of which introduce points of failure. Configuration Translation Prettier stores options in .prettierrc as a flat object. Biome groups formatter options under a formatter key in the configuration file and uses different names for some settings. Prettier config: { "printWidth" : 80 , "semi" : true , "singleQuote" : false , "trailingComma" : "es5" } Biome equivalent: { "formatter" : { "lineWidth" : 80 , "indentStyle" : "space" } , "javascript" : { "formatter" : { "semicolons" : "always" , "quoteStyle" : "double" , "trailingCommas" : "es5" } } } The printWidth option becomes lineWidth , and the quote and semicolon settings move into a nested javascript.formatter object. ESLint rules translate to Biome's linter.rules object, but only the rules Biome supports. Teams must audit their .eslintrc and extract the unsupported rules into a separate minimal ESLint config. Git History Preservation A formatting commit that touches thousands of lines pollutes git blame output unless the commit hash is added to .git-blame-ignore-revs . Without this step, every line's last edit shows the formatting commit instead of the functional change. Create .git-blame-ignore-revs : # Migrate to Biome formatter a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f8a9b0 Configure git to use the ignore file: git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs CI Pipeline Changes CI pipelines running prettier --check . and eslint . must switch to biome ci or split into biome check and a minimal eslint command for the remaining rules. Before migration (GitHub Actions): - name : Check formatting run : npx prettier --check . - name : Lint run : npx eslint . After migration: - name : Check formatting and lint run : npx @biomejs/biome ci - name : Lint React rules run : npx eslint --config .eslintrc.react.json . The biome ci command runs the formatter check and linter in a single pass, failing if either finds an issue. A pipeline translates config, updates hooks, adds blame ignore, and switches CI commands Rule Gaps and Missing Plugins: What Biome Still Cannot Cover in 2026 Biome's linter covers the core JavaScript and TypeScript rules but misses the ecosystem-specific checks that ESLint plugins provide. The gaps fall into three categories: React-specific rules, accessibility checks, and testing library rules. React-Specific Rules The eslint-plugin-react package enforces prop types, hooks dependencies, and JSX best practices. Biome does not replicate these rules as of version 2.0. Teams relying on hooks dependency checks (like react-hooks/exhaustive-deps ) must keep ESLint installed. Missing rules include: react/prop-types : enforces prop type validation react-hooks/rules-of-hooks : enforces hooks are called in the correct order react-hooks/exhaustive-deps : warns when effect dependencies are incomplete react/jsx-key : requires keys in list items Accessibility Checks The eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y package enforces ARIA roles, alt text on images, and keyboard navigation. Biome does not include these checks. Projects with accessibility requirements must run ESLint with the jsx-a11y plugin in parallel. Missing rules include: jsx-a11y/alt-text : requires alt text on images jsx-a11y/aria-role : enforces valid ARIA roles jsx-a11y/click-events-have-key-events : requires keyboard handlers alongside click handlers Testing Library Rules The eslint-plugin-testing-library package enforces best practices for React Testing Library, such as using screen queries and avoiding waitFor with side effects. Biome does not cover these rules. Missing rules include: testing-library/await-async-queries : requires await on async queries testing-library/no-wait-for-side-effects : disallows side effects inside waitFor Plugin Rules Biome covers Rules requiring ESLint eslint-plugin-react None All React-specific eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y None All accessibility eslint-plugin-testing-library None All testing rules The workaround is a dual-tool setup: Biome handles formatting and core linting, ESLint handles the plugin rules. A codebase runs Biome for core checks and ESLint for React-specific rules Real Migration: Step-by-Step Conversion Without Breaking Your Team's Workflow The migration follows a staged rollout: install Biome, run the formatter once, translate the config, and update CI. Step 1: Install Biome Install Biome as a dev dependency: npm install --save-dev @biomejs/biome Step 2: Run the Formatter Once Run the formatter to see the diff: npx @biomejs/biome format --write . Commit the formatting changes in a separate pull request with no functional changes. Step 3: Translate Configuration Create the configuration file from .prettierrc and .eslintrc : { "formatter" : { "lineWidth" : 80 } , "javascript" : { "formatter" : { "semicolons" : "always" , "quoteStyle" : "double" , "trailingCommas" : "es5" } } , "linter" : { "enabled" : true , "rules" : { "recommended" : true } } } Extract the unsupported ESLint rules into .eslintrc.react.json : { "extends" : [ "plugin:react/recommended" ] , "rules" : { "react-hooks/exhaustive-deps" : "warn" , "jsx-a11y/alt-text" : "error" } } Step 4: Update Pre-Commit Hooks Replace Prettier and ESLint in pre-commit hooks with Biome: Before: { "*.{js,ts,jsx,tsx}" : [ "prettier --write" , "eslint --fix" ] } After: { "*.{js,ts,jsx,tsx}" : [ "biome check --apply ." , "eslint --config .eslintrc.react.json --fix" ] } Step 5: Update CI Commands Replace Prettier and ESLint in CI with Biome: - name : Check formatting and lint run : npx @biomejs/biome ci - name : Lint React rules run : npx eslint --config .eslintrc.react.json . Step 6: Add Git Blame Ignore Add the formatting commit hash to .git-blame-ignore-revs and configure git to use it: git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs The staged rollout isolates failures to individual steps, making rollback straightforward. Migration workflow diagram Performance Benchmarks: Does Biome 2.0 Actually Save Time in Large Codebases Biome's Rust implementation runs faster than Prettier's JavaScript and ESLint's Node.js runtime, but the speed difference matters only if the team is not forced to run both tools in parallel. Benchmark Setup The benchmark uses a TypeScript monorepo with 120,000 lines of code across 400 files. The machine is a MacBook Pro M2 with 16GB RAM. Each tool runs three times, and the median time is recorded. Tool Median time Relative speed Prettier alone 4.2s 1x ESLint alone 12.8s 3x slower Prettier + ESLint 17.0s 4x slower Biome (format + lint) 1.1s 3.8x faster Biome + ESLint (React) 13.9s 1.2x faster Biome alone is 3.8 times faster than Prettier alone and 15.5 times faster than Prettier plus ESLint. When teams keep ESLint for React rules, the combined time drops to 13.9 seconds, only 1.2 times faster than the original setup. The speed gain is real when Biome replaces both tools, but projects with React-specific linting needs see a smaller benefit because ESLint still runs. A benchmark compares Prettier alone, ESLint alone, both together, Biome alone, and Biome with ESLint Performance benchmark chart Production Readiness Verdict: When to Migrate and When to Wait Biome 2.0 is production-ready for projects that do not depend on ESLint plugins, specifically greenfield TypeScript codebases and backend services. React projects or any codebase requiring accessibility checks must run Biome alongside ESLint, which reduces the speed benefit. Migrate immediately if: The project is TypeScript-only with no React or framework-specific linting needs The team can tolerate a one-time formatting commit that touches thousands of lines CI performance matters and the team is willing to maintain the configuration file instead of .prettierrc and .eslintrc Wait if: The codebase relies on React-specific rules like react-hooks/exhaustive-deps or accessibility checks from jsx-a11y The team cannot isolate a formatting commit or preserve git blame history The CI pipeline is already fast enough that saving 10-15 seconds per run does not justify the migration effort For teams in the middle, the hybrid setup (Biome for formatting and core linting, ESLint for plugin rules) works as a stepping stone until Biome's ecosystem catches up. Frequently Asked Questions Does Biome 2.0 produce identical output to Prettier? Biome matches Prettier on 95% of real-world code according to the Biome documentation , but edge cases like JSX line breaks, trailing commas, and import sorting differ. The first formatting commit shows the differences. Can Biome replace ESLint entirely in a React project? No. Biome does not cover React-specific rules from eslint-plugin-react or accessibility checks from eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y . React projects must keep ESLint running with a minimal config for the missing rules. How much faster is Biome than Prettier and ESLint combined? Benchmarks on a 120,000-line codebase show Biome running 15.5 times faster than Prettier plus ESLint when it replaces both. When ESLint stays in the pipeline for React rules, the combined time is only 1.2 times faster than the original setup. What happens to git blame after a formatting commit? A formatting commit that touches thousands of lines pollutes git blame output unless the commit hash is added to .git-blame-ignore-revs . Configure git to use the ignore file with git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs . Is the Biome configuration format stable? The configuration schema is stable as of version 2.0 according to the Biome configuration documentation , but the nesting structure differs from Prettier's flat .prettierrc . Teams must translate the config manually. Biome 2.0 delivers on the speed promise but not the full ESLint replacement. Greenfield TypeScript projects gain a faster, simpler toolchain. React projects gain faster formatting but keep ESLint for the gaps. The migration is a tradeoff: less tooling complexity and faster CI in exchange for maintaining a dual-tool setup until the ecosystem catches up. Projects that can live with the gaps should migrate now. Projects that cannot should wait for the React plugin support or accept the hybrid setup as the new baseline. What actually changes AI video output: notes on input structure, models, and duration
summary: Summary: In browser-based AI video tools, output quality tracks the structure of the input far more than the choice of model. Three observations, two limits, and the caveats that come with a small, uncontrolled sample. The questions that come up most often around generative video are which model to pick, how long a clip should be, and why a reasonable-sounding prompt produced an unusable result. This note collects observations from using King AI ( king-ai.net ), a browser tool for short clips, alongside public documentation of the models it exposes. It is not a benchmark. 1. Input structure dominates prompt wording An early version of the tool had a single prompt field. Typical inputs named the product and the intent, with nothing about the camera, the framing, or what had to remain recognizable. Clips moved, but they were rarely usable, and the failures were hard to explain to the person who wrote the prompt. Splitting the input into three explicit modes changed the failure rate more than any prompt guidance added afterwards: Text to video , when there is no reference material yet. Image to video , when an object's appearance has to survive the motion. First and last frame , when the edit requires a defined start and end. The mechanism is not mysterious. An image-to-video request carries identity information a sentence cannot: material, proportions, lighting direction. A first-and-last-frame request constrains trajectory, which removes a large part of the search space. In both cases the prompt does less work and the constraint does the rest. The practical implication: before rewriting a prompt for the third time, check whether the input mode is the actual problem. 2. Model choice shows up in motion character, not in "quality" Comparing several models on the same brief, the differences that matter are consistent but narrow: how a slow camera move resolves, whether a subject's gait looks mechanical, how quickly textures degrade as the camera travels. On a static product shot, the gap between models is often smaller than the gap between two prompts. That is a poor fit for a ranked list. Model selection behaves more like choosing a lens: the useful question is which motion vocabulary the shot needs, not which model scores higher in the abstract. It is also why per-model documentation is worth the maintenance cost; a name in a dropdown carries no information about motion style. The Kling model page is one example of that format: what the model is good at, which inputs it expects, and where it degrades. 3. Duration is the constraint that is easiest to ignore Coherence degrades with clip length well before the maximum supported length. Short shots hold; longer ones accumulate drift in geometry, lighting, or subject identity. A four-second default makes sense for evaluation: long enough to judge a camera move, short enough that comparisons stay cheap. Resolution trades against iteration speed the same way. A first pass at a lower resolution is usually the better use of a generation, with the higher setting reserved for output. Limits of this account Two, at least. First, the sample is not controlled: sessions differ in brief quality, subject matter, and reviewer tolerance, and there is no blind A/B or inter-rater measurement. Second, "usable" is a judgement, not a metric. A rigorous version would need paired briefs, blinded review, and per-model latency and cost recorded alongside. What is worth measuring next Blind pairwise review of the same brief across models, with reviewers who did not write the prompt. Failure taxonomy by clip length, so "coherence" stops being one bucket. Retention of subject identity measured against the reference image, not judged by eye. None of this is specific to one product. The general point is that the input contract and the shot length do more than the model leaderboard, and both are cheaper to change.

title: Discount Calculator: Why "Extra 20% Off the Sale Price" Isn't 50% Off
summary: Discount Calculator: Why "Extra 20% Off the Sale Price" Isn't 50% Off Last holiday season our small storefront ran a "30% off everything" sale and, on top of that, emailed a coupon for "an extra 20% off at checkout." Within a day, support had a pile of tickets that all said the same thing: a $120 jacket should be $60 with half off, so why did the checkout page show $67.20? The answer, of course, is that the two discounts multiply instead of add. But explaining that one-on-one, over and over, got old fast. So I wrote the math down three ways: a Python script for the team, a spreadsheet formula for support, and a browser page for anyone who just wants the number. Here's all three, plus the traps I hit along the way. The scenario The numbers from one real ticket: Jacket price: $120.00 Store sale: 30% off Coupon: extra 20% off (applied to the sale price, per the terms) Customer expected: $60.00 (30% + 20% = 50% off) Checkout showed: $67.20 $67.20 is correct. 30% off leaves 70% of the price; the extra 20% takes 80% of that . The total discount is 1 − (0.7 × 0.8) = 44%, not 50%. On a $120 jacket that's $18.80 more than the customer guessed, which is exactly the size of disappointment that turns into a ticket. Method 1: Python with Decimal (Python 3.11.1) Money in floats is asking for trouble, so I used Decimal . This is the script I ended up pasting into support replies (Python 3.11.1, standard library only): # stack_discounts.py — Python 3.11.1 from decimal import Decimal , ROUND_HALF_UP def final_price ( base : Decimal , percents : list [ Decimal ] ) -> Decimal : price = base for p in percents : price = price * ( Decimal ( "100" ) - p ) / Decimal ( "100" ) return price . quantize ( Decimal ( "0.01" ) , rounding = ROUND_HALF_UP ) base = Decimal ( "120.00" ) print ( final_price ( base , [ Decimal ( "30" ) , Decimal ( "20" ) ] ) ) # 67.20 print ( base * Decimal ( "50" ) / Decimal ( "100" ) ) # 60.00 (what the customer expected) effective = 100 - ( 100 - 30 ) * ( 100 - 20 ) / 100 print ( f "effective discount: {effective}%" ) # effective discount: 44.0% Running it prints 67.20 , 60.00 , and 44.0% . That last line became the one-liner I put in the coupon terms page. The Python decimal docs cover the rounding modes if you need banker's rounding instead of ROUND_HALF_UP . Method 2: JavaScript (Node 22.13.1) Our checkout is JavaScript, so I reproduced the same math there (Node 22.13.1): // discount.js — Node 22.13.1 const base = 120.0 ; const stacked = base * 0.7 * 0.8 ; console . log ( stacked ) ; // 67.2 console . log ( stacked . toFixed ( 2 ) ) ; // "67.20" console . log ( 100 - 0.7 * 0.8 * 100 ) ; // 44.00000000000001 Same result, one new problem: 100 - 0.7 * 0.8 * 100 comes out as 44.00000000000001 . Harmless here, but floats will bite you on prices that don't divide cleanly. A classic from our own test suite: 4.35 * 0.9 evaluates to 3.9149999999999996 , and (4.35 * 0.9).toFixed(2) returns "3.91" , not the 3.92 you'd get by rounding half up on paper. The usual fix is to work in integer cents and round once at the end, or reach for a decimal library. The toFixed docs on MDN spell out why the rounding is not what you'd expect from school math. For support staff, the plain-spreadsheet version ended up being enough: =ROUND(120 * (1 - 0.30) * (1 - 0.20), 2) → 67.20 Method 3: a browser tool when you just need the number Most of the time nobody wants a script. When a customer emails "what will I actually pay?", support opens a free online discount calculator , types in the original price and the discount, and reads off the final price and the savings. For stacked coupons you run it twice: take the first result as the new base for the second discount. It runs entirely in the browser, so there's nothing to install and nothing uploaded, which matters when the conversation involves someone's actual order. I also keep this browser-based tool pinned while writing promo copy, because it catches the "50% off!" claim before it ships instead of after. Three traps worth knowing 1. Adding percentages instead of stacking them. This is the whole ticket pile in one bullet. 30% + 20% is not 50% off; the real discount is 44%. I verified the direction the other way too: a 20% coupon followed by a 30% sale also lands on $67.20; stacking is commutative, which surprises people but follows straight from multiplication. 2. Trusting toFixed(2) to round "correctly." The 4.35 * 0.9 case above produced "3.91" where a human would write 3.92 , because the float closest to 3.915 is actually slightly below it. If your receipts must match the accountant's, compute in cents with integers: Math.round(435 * 90 / 100) gives 392 cents. Same input, different cent, real dispute. 3. Rounding per item versus at cart level. A cart with $9.99, $14.99, and $7.25 at 15% off rounds to $27.39 if you round each discounted item and sum, but $27.40 if you sum first and round once. One cent, but our payment provider rejected a settlement batch over exactly this class of mismatch. Pick one policy, write it down, and apply it everywhere. And check your jurisdiction: in some places sales tax is computed on the pre-discount price, so the receipt legitimately shows more than "price after discount" suggests. That's another source of tickets that no amount of discount math fixes. Quick summary Situation Correct math $120 base Single 30% off base × 0.70 $84.00 30% then extra 20% base × 0.70 × 0.80 $67.20 "50% off" (what customers expect) base × 0.50 $60.00 Effective stacked discount 1 − 0.70 × 0.80 44% The one-line takeaway: stacked discounts multiply, so convert each to its remainder and multiply those. Whether you do it in Python, in a spreadsheet, or in the discount calculator , do it before the coupon email goes out. Future-you in the support inbox will be grateful. title: Installing GDOM with a PostgreSQL Resource Library for GBase 8a
summary: GDOM (GBase Database Operation Manager), the China-domestically developed operations tool from GBASE, supports both PostgreSQL and mysql as its resource library as of 3.2B2 . This post records an install backed by an existing third-party PostgreSQL instance. From GDOM 3.7.0 onward PostgreSQL can be installed automatically, so use the bundled one if no external instance is available. The test instance was postgresql14-14.9-2PGDG.rhel7.x86_64.rpm and had to be installed beforehand . Everything below runs from the unpacked installer directory. Prerequisites Without expect the shell scripts will not run: yum install expect ./gdomSetupRPM.sh redhat7-x86_64 Supported OS types are redhat7-x86_64 , redhat8-x86_64 , kylin10-x86_64 and kylin10-aarch64 . Configuring demo.options The parameters that matter (full reference is in README.PDF inside the package): # Install directory; create it first and make sure user has access gdomRoot =/ opt / gdom gdomService = 10.0 . 2.103 # nginx sits in front, so 8080 is not the public port gdomServicePort = 8080 # Use a dedicated OS user, not an existing one user = gdom # Third-party PostgreSQL: leave gdomDb empty gdomDb = gdomDbPort = 5432 gdomDbUser = postgres gdomDbPwd = 625562 gdomDbDriver = org . postgresql . Driver # Setting gdomDbUrl overrides gdomDb. # This JDBC URL MUST NOT include a database name, or the install cannot connect. gdomDbUrl = 'jdbc:postgresql://10.0.2.103:5432/?useUnicode=true&characterEncoding=utf8&zeroDateTimeBehavior=convertToNull&allowPublicKeyRetrieval=true&useSSL=true&serverTimezone=GMT%2B8&allowMultiQueries=true' # Analysis store uses 6258 because 5258 is already taken by the local cluster gdomGBaseDb = 10.0 . 2.103 gdomGBaseDbPort = 6258 gdomGBaseDbUser = gbase2 gdomGBaseDbPwd = gbase2 gdomNginx = 10.0 . 2.103 gdomNginxPort = 8810 gdomRedis = 10.0 . 2.103 gdomRedisPort = 7481 gdomMq = 10.0 . 2.103 gdomMqPort = 9876 gdomDashBoardPort = 9898 If a database name slips into the URL, fix it afterwards in gdom/install/gdom-service/config/application.properties . Configuring mutual trust Run as root ; the script creates the OS user named by user and sets up SSH trust, prompting once for the root password and once for the gdom password: ./gdomMutualTrust.sh -a It distributes keys with ssh-copy-id . If you hit /usr/bin/ssh-copy-id: ERROR: invalid option (-f) , edit gdomTrust.exp and remove the -f flag after ssh-copy-id . Installing Move the package under the install user, fix ownership, then run the installer as that user: mv /root/GDOM-v3.2.0-build2-redhat7-x86_64 /home/gdom/GDOM-v3.2.0-build2-redhat7-x86_64 chown -R gdom:gdom /home/gdom/GDOM-v3.2.0-build2-redhat7-x86_64 su - gdom cd GDOM-v3.2.0-build2-redhat7-x86_64/ ./gdomInstall.sh -a The installer checks ports, distributes packages, unpacks and configures middleware, then initializes the stores. Port checks: 10.0.2.103 GDOM Service 8080 available Skipped, using third-party resource library <- GDOM DB Skipped, no HaProxy 10.0.2.103 GBase 6258 available 10.0.2.103 Nginx 8810 available 10.0.2.103 Redis 7481 available 10.0.2.103 Redis 9876 available <- RocketMQ Main packages shipped: gdom-service-3.2.0.tar.gz (216 MB) ​, jdk-1.8.0_411 (140 MB) ​, gdom-agent.tar.gz (130 MB) ​, GBase8a-NoLicense-9.5.3.28.11 (61 MB) ​ and rocketmq-all-5.2.0 (144 MB) ​, plus nginx 1.27.0 and redis 6.2.7. Configuration sets gbase_8a_gbase8a.cnf to port 6258 , points the master datasource at org.postgresql.Driver , and the analysis datasource at jdbc:gbase://10.0.2.103:6258/gdom_real . Resource-library initialization is skipped because a third-party database is in use, while the analysis stores gdom_real and gdom_history get their schemas and stored procedures created automatically. Initializing the PostgreSQL database Run two scripts with psql or another client — schema first, then data (adjust names to the actual directory): psql -d gdom -f /opt/gdom/install/sql/gdom_init_pg.sql psql -d gdom -f /opt/gdom/install/sql/gdom_init_pg_data.sql The installer log names the data script gdom_init_data_pg.sql , while the distribution listing and the command above use gdom_init_pg_data.sql ; use whichever file actually exists under /opt/gdom/install/sql . Starting, accessing and stopping ./gdomStart.sh -a # GBase / Redis / Nginx / RocketMQ / GDOM Service ./gdomStop.sh -s # stop GDOM Service Once startup finishes, open http://10.0.2.103:8810 . This install ran in a VM, so an IP mapping was used. Going forward, the interesting part is the split of responsibility: GDOM still orchestrates the whole middleware stack and the gbase analysis database, and only the resource-library step is left to the DBA. Later releases are expected to automate PostgreSQL initialization and fresh PostgreSQL installation as well, which would make the external database setup optional entirely.

title: Test swap: help my Android merge-idle game through Google Play closed testing (I test back)
summary: I'm a solo dev taking Moonbun Orbs through Google Play's closed testing (12 testers for 14 days). I already have 12, but people drop out, so I'm looking for a few more, and I'll gladly test your app back. What the game is A calm 2D merge-idle game set in space. Drag two matching orbs together to make a bigger one, from stardust all the way up to galaxies. No energy timers, and it keeps earning while you're away. How to join (Android phone + Gmail) Join the Google Group with the same Gmail your Play Store uses: https://groups.google.com/g/moonbun-orbs-testers Open https://play.google.com/apps/testing/com.moonbunstudio.orbmerge , tap Become a tester , then install from Google Play. Keep it installed for 14 days and open it now and then. No purchase is needed to play. Want a tester back? Comment your group link and opt-in link below. I'll join, install and open your app within 24 hours and reply with a screenshot. Things I learned running a closed test (might save you an hour) "Item not found" on the Play page right after opting in usually means Google hasn't synced yet. Waiting 10-30 minutes fixed it every time for my testers. The Gmail used for the Google Group and the one signed in to the Play Store app must be the same. Phones with two Google accounts are the most common cause of "I joined but can't download". Adding another Google Group to your tester list goes through review again, so batch it with your next release. Testers drop out. Aim for 15-20 so you don't fall below 12 and restart the 14 days. Found a bug? Post a screenshot in the comments and I'll look into it.

title: I almost gave up on local llms on low end hardware until I made these changes to my setup
summary: Squeezing Every Drop of Speed Out of a Laptop CPU: Recompiling ik_llama.cpp for Gemma 4 E2B + MTP + Pi After my previous findings, I almost called it quits on running models locally on my hardware: an AMD Ryzen 5 5625U with 16 GB dual-channel 3200 MHz RAM , locked to "Cool" mode with max processor state capped at 99% (~10–12W power limit, no turbo spikes). Before giving up, I looked into ternary models. I tried running Ternary Bonsai 2 9B , and it gave me similar performance to my Qwen 3.5 4B & 2B setup—around 6–10 tokens/sec (specifically ~6 tok/s on Bonsai). Token generation was still pretty slow. It wasn't horrible, but it wasn't great either. Then I saw a YouTube video about Gentoo Linux —the distro where you compile almost all software directly on your own hardware for a small performance boost. It reminded me of Formula 1: in F1, even shaving a few hundredths of a second off a lap time can be the difference between winning and losing. So I decided to recompile the inference engine myself. I ended up recompiling ikawrakow/ik_llama.cpp specifically for my Zen 3 CPU ( -O3 -march=znver3 -mtune=znver3 ) because it supports -rtr (run-time repacking) . In simple terms, -rtr reorganizes the model's weights in RAM into a neat 8-row interleaved layout tailored for Zen 3's AVX2 vector instructions, so the CPU can read and multiply weights much faster instead of unpacking them awkwardly on the fly. Choosing the Right Model & Tuning Threads After consulting with Gemini Hydrogen , I decided to go with Gemma 4 E2B (essentially ~4.6B total parameters / ~2.3B active compute). For my 16 GB dual-channel RAM setup, this hits the sweet spot for speed and accuracy. Even though its standalone coding isn't quite as strong as Qwen 3.5 4B with thinking on, it works great for my workflow because I use Hydrogen in Antigravity as the cloud orchestrator and run Gemma 4 locally with thinking turned off . The performance genuinely surprised me—I did not expect it to run this well on a 10–12W laptop cap. Because of the Cool-mode power limit, I ran llama-bench ( -ngl 0 -rtr 1 --no-mmap -fa 1 -p 512 -n 128 ) across 3, 4, 5, and 6 threads to find the sweet spot: Threads Prompt Processing ( pp512 ) Token Generation ( tg128 ) -t 3 111.69 tok/s 9.07 tok/s -t 4 142.74 tok/s 9.00 tok/s -t 5 166.83 tok/s 7.84 tok/s -t 6 143.93 tok/s 6.70 tok/s Using all 6 threads starved per-core clocks under the 10–12W cap and dropped generation to 6.70 tok/s . Splitting it to -t 4 for generation and -tb 5 for prompt processing gave me the best of both worlds. I'm sure if I switched to Performance or Balanced mode at 100% power it would get an even bigger boost, but I don't want to melt my laptop. Initially, I ran google_gemma-4-E2B-it-IQ4_NL.gguf ( 3.14 GiB , from bartowski ) because it uses slightly less RAM with similar accuracy, paired with the mtp-gemma-4-E2B-it-Q8_0.gguf ( ~95 MiB ) MTP speculative drafter. Even though the drafter cancelled out the small RAM savings, it was still much lighter than running a bigger model with MTP—and it hit 17.31 tok/s with a 94.1% draft acceptance rate (16/17 accepted) on a smoke test. Switching to the Uncensored Model Around a day later, I saw a video by Kai on YouTube about uncensored models and decided it made more sense to run the uncensored variant. I switched to: Main Model: gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-q4_0-unquantized-heretic.i1-Q4_0.gguf ( 3.12 GiB , from mradermacher , skipping mmproj to save RAM) MTP Drafter: gemma-4-E2B-it-assistant-Q8_0.gguf ( 94.81 MiB , from cafkafk ) The performance is fantastic: MTP Draft Acceptance Rate: 80.77% (21 accepted / 26 generated on JSON test) Token Generation: 13.04 – 15.39 tok/s (300 tokens of Python code in ~23s) Prompt Processing: 112.70 – 172.69 tok/s Memory Footprint: ~3.77 GB total ( 3181.5 MiB model + q8_0 KV cache at 16K context) + ~371 MB for the drafter, with all 271 main tensors and 23 drafter tensors repacked via -rtr . Launch Profiles & Offline Pi Harness I set up two .bat launchers—one with thinking turned off for when Hydrogen is orchestrating, and another with thinking turned on for standalone debugging: Shared Engine & Low-RAM Flags: - m "E:\models\gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-q4_0-unquantized-heretic.i1-Q4_0.gguf" ^ - md "E:\models\gemma-4-E2B-it-assistant-Q8_0.gguf" ^ -- spec - type mtp : n_max = 2 , p_min = 0.0 ^ - rtr -- no - mmap - ngl 0 - t 4 - tb 5 - c 16384 - np 1 ^ - ctk q8_0 - ctv q8_0 - fa on - b 512 - ub 256 -- jinja -- host 127.0 . 0.1 -- port 8080 (Using -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 halves KV cache memory, -np 1 keeps context to a single slot so RAM stays low, and --spec-type mtp:n_max=2,p_min=0.0 caps draft guesses at 2 so the CPU doesn't waste cycles verifying rejected tokens.) Thinking OFF ( start-gemma4-uncensored.bat — Fast Coding / Cloud-Orchestrated): --reasoning off --temp 0.4 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 64 --repeat-penalty 1.1 Thinking ON ( start-gemma4-uncensored-thinking.bat — Complex Debugging): --reasoning on --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 64 --repeat-penalty 1.0 I also set up Pi ( @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent ) with itayinbarr/little-coder (for just-in-time tool injection and small-model guardrails), the Pi Code GUI extension in VS Code, and a custom Pi extension that sandboxes file and bash tools strictly to my E:\ flash drive—so I still have a capable local coding assistant even when I'm offline or don't have access to cloud models. Looking forward to seeing what this uncensored local setup can help me build and create. Repo with all launch scripts & Pi configs: https://github.com/MVYNE06/gemma4-zen3-local-stack

title: Why CSS 1in = 96px Is Not 1 Physical Inch (Building a True 1:1 Screen Ruler in React)
summary: If you have ever tried setting width: 1in; or width: 10cm; in CSS and held a physical ruler up to your monitor, you probably noticed something frustrating: it is almost never 1 physical inch. On a 27-inch 4K monitor, a 13-inch MacBook Air, and a 6.7-inch Android phone, 1in in CSS can be off by 15% to 45% . Here is why browsers cannot reliably report physical millimeters out of the box, and how we built a true 1:1 actual-size online ruler and ring sizer in React using ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 credit-card PPI calibration . Why 1in , 1cm , and window.devicePixelRatio Cannot Give True Physical Size According to the W3C CSS Values and Units specification, 1in is locked to exactly 96 CSS pixels ( 1cm = 37.795px , 1mm = 3.7795px ). Wait - what about window.devicePixelRatio ? devicePixelRatio only tells you how many hardware pixels map to 1 CSS pixel (for example, 2 on Retina displays or 2.75 on high-DPI phones). It still does not tell JavaScript the physical diagonal size of the monitor or phone glass in inches! Browsers deliberately omit raw physical display dimensions (EDID data) to reduce browser fingerprinting . As a result: Display CSS 1in Real Physical Size of 96 CSS px Error Standard 24" 1080p Monitor 96px ~1.04 in +4% 13.3" MacBook Retina ( 2x ) 96px ~0.84 in -16% 6.5" Smartphone ( 3x ) 96px ~0.66 in -34% So if you build a browser ruler using static CSS cm or in units, it will be visibly wrong on almost every laptop and smartphone. The Reliable Fix: ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 Credit-Card Calibration Almost every person on Earth has a globally standardized physical reference object in their wallet: a standard bank card, debit card, or ID card . Under the ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 international standard, every standard payment card has the exact same physical width: Width: 85.60 mm ( 8.56 cm / 3.370 inches ) Height: 53.98 mm ( 5.398 cm / 2.125 inches ) Instead of guessing the user's screen PPI, let the user hold a bank card flat against the screen and drag a slider until an on-screen card box matches the physical card edge-to-edge. Once cardWidthPx matches 3.37 physical inches, calculating the exact effective CSS Pixels Per Inch (PPI) takes one line of math: const STANDARD_CARD_INCHES = 3.37 ; // 85.60 mm (ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1) export function calculateEffectivePpi ( cardWidthPx : number ) : number { return cardWidthPx / STANDARD_CARD_INCHES ; } From that single calibrated ppi number, every physical unit becomes exact on that display: export function pxToPhysical ( px : number , ppi : number ) { const inches = px / ppi ; return { inches : Number ( inches . toFixed ( 2 ) ) , cm : Number ( ( inches * 2.54 ) . toFixed ( 2 ) ) , mm : Number ( ( inches * 25.4 ) . toFixed ( 1 ) ) , } ; } Persist that calibrated ppi in localStorage , and the user only ever has to calibrate once per device: const STORAGE_KEY = "omnitools_ruler_ppi" ; export function loadSavedPpi ( ) : number { try { const saved = localStorage . getItem ( STORAGE_KEY ) ; const parsed = saved ? parseFloat ( saved ) : NaN ; return Number . isFinite ( parsed ) && parsed >= 40 && parsed <= 300 ? parsed : 96 ; } catch { return 96 ; } } (Clamping between 40 and 300 prevents corrupted storage values from breaking the UI.) Bonus Use Case: An On-Screen Ring Size Finder (US, UK, and India Sizes) Once you know the true ppi of a screen, you can measure more than straight lines. You can render a calibrated circle where the user places an existing ring directly onto their phone or laptop glass and adjusts the circle diameter until it aligns with the inside edge of the ring: interface RingSizeEntry { mm : number ; us : string ; uk : string ; india : string ; } const RING_SIZES : RingSizeEntry [ ] = [ { mm : 14.9 , us : "4" , uk : "H" , india : "8" } , { mm : 15.7 , us : "5" , uk : "J 1/2" , india : "10" } , { mm : 16.5 , us : "6" , uk : "M" , india : "12" } , { mm : 17.3 , us : "7" , uk : "O" , india : "14" } , { mm : 18.2 , us : "8" , uk : "Q" , india : "17" } , { mm : 19.0 , us : "9" , uk : "S" , india : "19" } , { mm : 19.8 , us : "10" , uk : "T 1/2" , india : "22" } , { mm : 20.6 , us : "11" , uk : "V 1/2" , india : "25" } , ] ; export function matchRingSize ( diameterPx : number , ppi : number ) { const diameterMm = ( diameterPx / ppi ) * 25.4 ; const closest = RING_SIZES . reduce ( ( prev , curr ) => Math . abs ( curr . mm - diameterMm ) < Math . abs ( prev . mm - diameterMm ) ? curr : prev ) ; return { diameterMm : Number ( diameterMm . toFixed ( 1 ) ) , closest } ; } 3 Frontend Edge Cases to Watch Out For Browser Zoom ( Ctrl + / Ctrl - ): Remind users to keep browser zoom at 100% during calibration and measurement, because zooming scales CSS pixels without changing localStorage . Prevent Accidental Text Selection While Dragging Markers: Add select-none ( user-select: none ) and touch-action: none on draggable measurement handles so mobile Safari/Chrome does not scroll the viewport while dragging a marker. Sub-Pixel Rendering for 1mm Ticks: On standard displays, 1mm is roughly 3.78px . Always compute tick positions from mm * (ppi / 25.4) instead of rounding each step cumulatively, otherwise rounding drift compounds to 2-3mm across a 15cm ruler! Try the Live Browser Implementation We built this full calibrated ruler, dual red/blue measurement markers (horizontal and vertical), and US/UK/India ring sizer completely client-side with zero tracking or app downloads: Online Ruler (Actual Size 1:1 + Ring Size Finder): https://omnitools.net/tools/online-ruler Unit Converter (Length, Weight, Temp & Storage): https://omnitools.net/tools/unit-converter Have you ever run into CSS physical-unit bugs on HiDPI screens or print stylesheets? Drop your experience in the comments!

title: AI Isn't Transforming Work, Because the System Hasn't Changed
summary: The speed is real. The change is not. A draft that took an hour now takes ten minutes. A summary arrives in seconds. A first version of anything is one prompt away. And yet the week feels the same. The same meetings. The same rework. That gap is the subject of this piece. AI is doing real work at the level of the single task. It is not, on its own, changing how work moves through a team. Those are two different things, and most teams have only touched the first one. A New Shape for Work opens with a plain diagnosis. AI is helpful, but it has not transformed the way most teams operate. The difference feels marginal. The reason, the guidebook says, is leverage. Used without a clear strategy, AI gives surprisingly little of it. The image the guidebook uses is a bicycle with one gear. "It's like adding a power boost to a bicycle with only one gear," the Introduction says, "the pedals move frenetically, but nothing has fundamentally changed." The pedals spin faster. The bike goes no faster. The rider works harder and arrives at the same place. Leverage is what lets you move up a level. The guidebook puts it this way: "Increased leverage allows you to move up to a higher level, and work on the system rather than in the system." That sentence is the whole argument in one line. Working in the system means doing the tasks faster. Working on the system means changing how the tasks flow and what survives them. Before and after The guidebook draws the contrast as a before and after list. Before: information scattered everywhere; everyone reinventing their own wheel; agents confused by outdated docs; one-off chats; isolated achievements. After: everything automatically organized; rationalized, shared systems; clean context for agents; automated processes; compounding flywheel. Read that list slowly. Nothing on the before side is a complaint about AI being weak. The AI works. The system around it does not. Outdated docs confuse agents. Scattered information means every task starts from zero. One-off chats mean nothing learned on Monday helps on Tuesday. Isolated achievements mean one person's win stays one person's win. The after side is not about a smarter model. It is about a shared system that holds what the team knows, so the model has something solid to work with. Organization comes first, automation second. That order matters. Automating a mess gives you a faster mess. Think about your own week. How much of it goes to finding things, re-explaining things, and redoing things? That is the tax of a system that has not changed. AI can cut the time each task takes, but it cannot cut the tax. Only a change to the system can do that. A faster draft does not fix a slow approval. A faster summary does not fix a meeting that should not exist. This is why the guidebook refuses to sell AI as a tool upgrade. A tool upgrade makes the same work faster. A system change makes different work possible. The first feels like progress for a month and then stalls. The second is slower to start and keeps paying. The core philosophy The guidebook states its core philosophy in plain terms: "Humans thrive when we do the creative work that we love, and that only we can do. Everything else can, should, and eventually will be automated." The question is how. The path has two parts. First, create a shared context system that your whole team and their agents can work in together. Second, create shared AI systems, sometimes called factories, that a handful of people can be responsible for, and that everyone else can benefit from. That sounds large. The guidebook insists it is not. The simplest version, it says, is nothing more than a shared to-do list with an agent and your team. That takes a few minutes to set up, and it can grow to handle tasks of near-infinite complexity. You do not need to change everything overnight. Start with one workflow, or one team. See if it works. Then go from there. That is the practical test hidden inside the philosophy. If the only place AI touches your work is inside private chats, the system has not changed. If one shared list exists, and an agent works from it, and the whole team can see the result, the system has started to change. When one part of a team adopts this way of working, the guidebook says, the rest quickly follow, without need for persuasion or change management. That claim is easy to test. It either happens or it does not. But it points to the real measure of success: not whether individuals use AI, but whether the team works differently because of it. What to do with this Pick one repeated piece of work. A weekly update. A status report. A triage step that happens every day. Give it a shared home instead of a private chat. Put the instructions and the expected output in one place the team can see. Let an agent run it from there. Watch what breaks, fix that one thing, and run it again. Do that, and you will learn more about your system in a week than a year of faster drafts will teach you. The drafts were never the problem. The system was. AI is not failing at work. It is waiting for the system to change. The bicycle needs another gear. The Matrix framed the same choice years ago. The blue pill is the faster draft in the same system. The red pill is changing the system itself. Transformation is a choice, not a tool swap.

title: GitHub Actions runner pricing per minute in 2026: the rate table, larger runners, self-hosted costs and nine billing traps
summary: How much does a GitHub Actions runner cost per minute? In November 2026, GitHub’s hosted Linux x64 runners cost $0.006 a minute at 2 vCPU, $0.012 at 4 vCPU and $0.022 at 8 vCPU, per GitHub’s Actions runner pricing reference; the 4 and 8 vCPU larger runners need GitHub Team or Enterprise Cloud. Sengi Basic runs the same Linux x64 jobs for $0.001, $0.002 and $0.004 a minute, one-sixth of GitHub’s rate at 2 vCPU, with 3,000 free Basic minutes a month; Sengi Premium costs $0.003, $0.006 and $0.012. The rate is only part of the bill: nine traps below, from dollar allowances and per-job rounding to plan fees, cache fees and runs nobody cancelled, change what you pay. Last checked November 11, 2026 : GitHub’s runner pricing reference and Actions billing documentation re-read that day with no change, and Sengi’s rates against its published pricing. Other providers’ rates and terms as read on November 7, 2026 from each provider’s own pricing page and docs. We list only what a provider states; where a page is silent, we say so. GitHub Actions runner pricing per minute: the November 2026 table GitHub’s hosted Linux x64 rates next to both Sengi runner classes at matched vCPU counts, in US dollars per minute at list price. Linux x64 size GitHub hosted Sengi Premium Sengi Basic Sengi Basic label 2 vCPU $0.006 $0.003 $0.001 sengi-basic-2-ubuntu-2404 4 vCPU $0.012 $0.006 $0.002 sengi-basic-4-ubuntu-2404 8 vCPU $0.022 $0.012 $0.004 sengi-basic-8-ubuntu-2404 At every size Sengi Basic is the lowest rate per minute and Sengi Premium is about half of GitHub’s. To price your own month, put your minutes into the GitHub Actions cost calculator; the cheapest runners table adds every other hosted runner. What does a GitHub Actions Linux 2-core runner cost per minute? GitHub’s standard Linux 2-core x64 runner, the machine behind ubuntu-latest in a private repository, costs $0.006 a minute with 8 GB of memory: $6 per 1,000 minutes once the plan’s included usage is spent. Sengi Basic at 2 vCPU costs $0.001 a minute with 8 GB, $1 per 1,000 minutes; Sengi Premium costs $0.003, $3 per 1,000. The 2-core runner is where most minutes go: lint, unit tests, type checks, small builds and the checks AI coding agents trigger on every pull request. That makes the 2 vCPU rate the one number that moves a CI bill most. GitHub larger runners pricing per minute: 4-core and 8-core GitHub calls anything above the standard runner a larger runner, and offers them only to organizations on GitHub Team or Enterprise Cloud. On Linux x64 it lists 4-core at $0.012 a minute and 8-core at $0.022: the 8-core rate is 3.7 times the 2-core rate. Each step up on Sengi doubles the price: Sengi Basic: $0.002 a minute at 4 vCPU and $0.004 at 8 vCPU, 18% of GitHub’s 8-core rate. Sengi Premium: $0.006 at 4 vCPU and $0.012 at 8 vCPU, 55% of GitHub’s 8-core rate. Both run on personal and organization repositories. GitHub larger runners vs third-party runners works out when a bigger runner pays for itself, and runner sizes lists every Sengi label. What a month of GitHub Actions minutes costs Per-minute rates hide how fast a bill grows. Each cell is the list rate times the minutes, before any included or free usage. Minutes a month GitHub hosted Sengi Premium Sengi Basic 1,000 at 2 vCPU $6 $3 $1 10,000 at 2 vCPU $60 $30 $10 10,000 at 4 vCPU $120 $60 $20 10,000 at 8 vCPU $220 $120 $40 100,000 at 2 vCPU $600 $300 $100 Sengi’s 3,000 free Basic minutes take $3 off a Basic month, and GitHub’s included usage, $12 to $300 by plan, comes off a GitHub month; trap 1 shows how far it goes. What 100,000 GitHub Actions minutes cost runs the sum on every hosted runner. Trap 1: included usage is dollars, and bigger runners spend it faster GitHub now states each plan’s included compute as a dollar amount, not minutes, and deducts each runner’s own rate from it. On GitHub Team and Enterprise Cloud, larger runners draw on it too: GitHub plan Included a month 2 vCPU minutes 4 vCPU minutes 8 vCPU minutes Free $12 2,000 Not available Not available Pro $18 3,000 Not available Not available Team $18 3,000 1,500 818 Enterprise Cloud $300 50,000 25,000 13,636 Allowances that count in 2 vCPU units shrink the same way elsewhere: Sengi’s 3,000 free Basic credits are 3,000 minutes at 2 vCPU, 1,500 at 4 and 750 at 8; Avrea’s 3,000 free minutes are used proportionally at larger sizes; Depot counts included minutes at 2× and 4× for 4 and 8 vCPU; Latchkey counts a 4 vCPU minute as two and an 8 vCPU minute as four. Compare allowances in dollars: Sengi’s is worth $3 a month, Avrea’s $12, GitHub Team’s $18. Trap 2: per-job rounding to the whole minute GitHub rounds the minutes and partial minutes each job uses up to the next whole minute. A matrix of 20 jobs that each run 61 seconds bills as 40 minutes, not 20.3. Latchkey also rounds up per job, and so does Sengi. Namespace bills a minimum of one minute and rounds the next 15 seconds down, so 70 seconds is one minute and 150 seconds is three. CRACI and tempus.build bill per second. title: Stop Building “Remote Controls.” Build an Automation Engine
summary: Most smart home projects stall at the same point. You buy a smart plug. You open the app. You tap a button. The lamp turns on. It feels like progress — until you realize you have built a very expensive remote control. The STONE article on smart home automation draws a distinction that every developer should internalize before writing a single line of integration code: a smart device responds to a command; an automated home evaluates a condition and acts without anyone asking. The gap between those two things is not hardware. It is architecture. The Loop You Are Actually Building A functioning automation system is a closed loop. Sensors produce state. A logic layer evaluates that state against rules. Actuators receive commands. The loop runs continuously, mostly without human input. In a developer-friendly stack, that loop maps cleanly onto three concerns: Ingestion: devices publish state to a message bus. Evaluation: a rule engine subscribes to that bus and decides what should happen. Dispatch: commands go back out to the devices that can change the physical world. The mistake is collapsing these into a single process. When your sensor firmware directly calls your light’s HTTP endpoint, you have created a point-to-point dependency that breaks the moment either device changes, goes offline, or gets replaced. The MQTT pub/sub model exists precisely to decouple these concerns: devices publish to a broker; the logic layer subscribes; neither side needs to know the other’s address. Home Assistant as the Evaluation Layer, Not the Whole System Home Assistant is often described as a “hub,” which undersells what it actually is. Architecturally, it is a local-first event loop that integrates thousands of device protocols — Matter, Zigbee, Z-Wave, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth — and exposes them as entities that automations can reason about. It is the evaluation layer. It is not the message bus, and it is not the device. The cleaner design separates them. Run an MQTT broker (Mosquitto is the obvious starting point) as the message backbone. Let devices — ESP32 sensors, Tasmota-flashed plugs, Zigbee bridges — publish state to that broker. Let Home Assistant subscribe, evaluate, and publish commands back. The result is a system where you can swap a Zigbee temperature sensor for a Wi-Fi one without rewriting the automation that depends on it, because the automation is subscribed to a topic, not to a device. MQTT Discovery Is the Glue Worth Learning The single highest-leverage implementation detail in this stack is MQTT Discovery. Instead of manually defining every sensor in configuration files, a device publishes a retained JSON payload to a discovery topic. Home Assistant picks it up and creates the entity automatically. A minimal discovery payload for a temperature sensor looks like this: Published to homeassistant/sensor/livingroom_temp/config, this payload registers the entity, binds it to a physical device, and makes it available to automations without any manual YAML. The device becomes self-describing. That property matters more than it first appears: it means the automation layer does not need to be redeployed when hardware changes. The Automation Itself Should Be Boring Once the plumbing is in place, automations should read like state machines, not scripts. A trigger fires on a state transition. Conditions constrain the context. Actions dispatch commands. This is deliberately unglamorous. It is also deterministic, idempotent, and debuggable. When it fails — and it will — you can inspect three separate concerns: did the sensor publish? did the condition evaluate correctly? did the action reach the actuator? The Real Lesson Smart home automation is not a hardware problem. The devices are cheap and increasingly interoperable. The hard part is resisting the urge to build point-to-point remote controls and instead investing in a decoupled loop where state flows into a bus, logic evaluates it, and commands flow back out. Build that loop once, and every device you add afterward becomes a new input or output — not a new integration project.

title: The Swap Is the Easy Part: What Really Happens Between Clicking Exchange and Receiving Your Tokens?
summary: TronSeven — Non-Custodial Token Swaps on TRON Network Swap TRC-20 tokens on TRON with self-custody and open-source smart contracts. Low fees, verifiable on TRONSCAN. tronseven.com Most crypto users have experienced the same moment. You select two tokens, enter an amount, check the estimated output, connect your wallet, and click Swap. A few seconds later, the transaction appears in your wallet history. Simple, right? But between that button click and the arrival of your tokens, several important things happen. Your wallet communicates with the blockchain, a smart contract executes instructions, network resources are consumed, and the resulting transaction becomes part of a public ledger. Understanding this process changes how you evaluate crypto swap platforms. Instead of asking only, "How quickly can I exchange these tokens?", a better question is: Can I understand and verify what happens to my assets during the exchange? Let's explore that question from a practical TRON ecosystem perspective. A Token Swap Is More Than a Price Conversion Traditional currency conversion is relatively easy to understand. You exchange one currency for another using an agreed exchange rate. Blockchain swaps introduce additional layers. When exchanging TRC-20 tokens on TRON, the process generally involves: A wallet that authorizes the transaction. Token contracts representing the assets. A smart contract responsible for executing the swap. Network resources required to process the transaction. Blockchain confirmation and transaction records. Each component has a different responsibility. The wallet authorizes actions. The smart contract executes predefined logic. The TRON network processes the transaction and records its result. This distinction matters because a user is not simply exchanging two numbers on a screen. They are authorizing an on-chain operation. What Happens After You Click Swap? Let's break the process into understandable stages. Stage One: Transaction preparation The interface collects the selected tokens, the amount, and the expected output. Depending on the protocol, it may also calculate a route, estimate price impact, and account for slippage. These values help the user understand the proposed transaction before signing. Stage Two: Wallet authorization The application requests permission from the connected wallet to submit the transaction. This is an important security checkpoint. A wallet signature should never be treated as a routine confirmation without understanding what is being authorized. Always review the transaction details and make sure the requested action matches your intention. Stage Three: Smart contract execution The transaction reaches the relevant smart contract. The contract processes the instructions according to its programmed logic. If the required conditions are satisfied, the exchange can execute. Otherwise, the transaction may fail. Stage Four: Blockchain confirmation The TRON network processes the transaction. Once confirmed, the resulting transaction can be inspected using a blockchain explorer such as TRONSCAN. This provides an independent way to examine what happened instead of relying exclusively on an application's interface. Why TRON Energy and Bandwidth Matter One interesting aspect of the TRON ecosystem is its resource model. TRON uses two important resources: Bandwidth Bandwidth is used to account for the size of transactions and the data they contain. Energy Energy is primarily required for executing smart contract operations. A token swap involving TRC-20 contracts can consume Energy, while the transaction itself also uses network resources. This is one reason why comparing swap services solely by their advertised exchange rates can be misleading. The real cost of an operation may involve several components: Network resource consumption. Liquidity-related costs. Price impact. Any applicable service fees. A transparent interface should help users understand the relevant costs before they authorize a transaction. Slippage: The Difference Between Expectation and Execution Imagine that you want to exchange 1,000 USDT for another token. The interface displays an estimated amount you should receive. However, blockchain transactions do not always execute at the exact price displayed when the transaction was prepared. Market conditions can change. Liquidity can shift. Other transactions can affect the execution price. This is where slippage becomes important. Slippage represents the difference between the expected execution price and the actual execution price. A user should understand the following concepts before confirming an exchange: Expected output: The estimated amount of tokens to receive. Minimum received: The minimum output accepted by the transaction, where applicable. Price impact: How the trade itself affects the available market price. Slippage tolerance: The permitted deviation from the expected execution conditions. Setting slippage too tightly can cause transactions to fail. Setting it too loosely can expose users to worse execution than anticipated. The goal is not to choose the largest tolerance. It is to understand the trade-off. Blockchain Transparency Is a Practical Security Tool One of the most valuable characteristics of public blockchains is that transactions can be independently inspected. For TRON users, TRONSCAN provides a way to investigate transaction records. Instead of trusting a notification saying that a swap was successful, users can examine the underlying transaction. Useful details include: Transaction status. Transaction hash. Contract interactions. Token transfers. Addresses involved. Block information. Resource consumption. This does not automatically prove that a protocol is safe. A successful transaction only confirms that the blockchain processed the operation. It does not establish that the smart contract has no vulnerabilities or that the service is trustworthy. That distinction is essential. Blockchain transparency is a verification tool, not a universal security guarantee. Five Questions to Ask Before Using Any Swap Platform Before connecting a wallet to a new exchange interface, consider these questions: Is the smart contract publicly identifiable? You should be able to locate the relevant contract address and inspect its on-chain activity. Can the contract source code be verified? Verified source code makes it easier for independent researchers to examine contract logic. Is there meaningful security documentation? Look for details about audits, their scope, the reviewed contract versions, and any disclosed limitations. An audit is useful evidence, but it is not a guarantee against future vulnerabilities. Are the transaction costs understandable? A clear interface should distinguish estimated output, network costs, price impact, and applicable fees. Do you retain control of your wallet? Understand whether a service is custodial or non-custodial, what permissions it requests, and what happens to your assets during execution. Never share your seed phrase or private keys with a swap service. The Future of Crypto Swaps Is About Better Decisions The next generation of crypto swap interfaces should not compete exclusively on speed. Speed matters, but it is only one part of the experience. Users also need: Clear transaction information. Understandable fee structures. Verifiable smart contracts. Better wallet interaction. Meaningful security documentation. Transparent execution details. The best swap experience is one where users understand what they are authorizing rather than blindly trusting a confirmation button. This is particularly important as the TRON ecosystem continues to support a growing range of tokens, applications, and decentralized financial activities. Final Thoughts A crypto swap may look like a simple exchange, but it represents a coordinated interaction between wallets, smart contracts, network resources, and blockchain infrastructure. Understanding these layers is one of the most useful skills a crypto user can develop. The next time you exchange tokens, take a moment to look beyond the displayed rate. Check the transaction. Understand the permissions. Review the contract. Verify the result. Because in decentralized finance, the ability to verify what happened is just as important as the ability to make it happen.

title: How to send HubSpot deal stages to the Meta Conversions API
summary: Your campaign records leads. HubSpot records who qualified and who bought. Unless something connects the two, Meta never learns which leads turned into customers, and keeps optimizing for whoever fills in the form. Key points When a deal changes stage in HubSpot, send an event to the Meta Conversions API: Qualified , Disqualified and Purchase with the deal amount. The identifiers that let Meta match the event ( fbc , fbp , or the Lead Ads ID) must be stored when the lead is created . They can't be recovered later. In HubSpot, store them on the contact , then follow the deal's association to read them. Use action_source: system_generated , custom_data.event_source: "crm" and a stable event_id per deal and stage. Check HubSpot's native Meta events first. If they cover your case, you may not need any code. Step 1: store the identifier when the lead is born This is the step that can't be fixed later. For leads from your site, save the _fbc and _fbp cookies, plus email and phone, into contact properties at submission. For leads from Meta's instant forms, save the leadgen_id . Create contact properties with clear internal names, for example meta_fbc , meta_fbp and meta_lead_id . Your code always uses the internal name, never the label. Two details catch most people: _fbc only exists when the visitor arrived with an fbclid in the URL, and it only works within the same domain. Step 2: detect stage changes With a HubSpot Service Key (legacy private apps can no longer be created), there are no webhooks, so a small bot polls the deals search endpoint every few minutes for deals modified since the last run, filtered by your pipeline. For each deal that reached a tracked stage, it reads the deal's associated contact and takes the identifiers from there. Compare stages by their internal ID ( closedwon , or a numeric ID in custom pipelines), never by label. Step 3: build the Conversions API event The payload has four details that decide whether Meta uses it: action_source is system_generated ; custom_data carries lead_event_source (your CRM name) and event_source: "crm" ; user_data has lead_id for instant-form leads, or fbc and fbp in plain text plus email and phone hashed with SHA-256; event_id is stable per deal and stage, like <deal id>_won , so a reprocessed run doesn't count twice. For Purchase, add value and currency from the deal. HubSpot returns amount as a string and it may be empty when the stage moves before the rep fills it in, so wait a cycle instead of sending zero. Step 4: keep outbound out of the signal If the same pipeline gets paid leads and prospecting or referral deals, check for a paid-origin mark before sending anything. Otherwise every outbound sale becomes a Purchase credited to your campaigns. Where to start Start with Purchase: it's the only event with real value. Add Qualified next. If your funnel closes few deals a month, keep the campaign optimizing on a higher-volume event and use Purchase to judge quality. The 4-Layer Tracking Kit has this bot ready in Python, built for HubSpot's 2026-03 API, plus the three layers before it (browser, web GTM and server-side GTM with deduplication) and a 12-step validation ladder. FAQ Isn't HubSpot's native Meta integration enough? Sometimes. HubSpot can send ad conversion events to Meta based on lifecycle stage changes and HubSpot form submissions, on Marketing Hub Starter and above. It doesn't cover deal stages in any pipeline, forms outside HubSpot or a pixel that lives in GTM with server-side tracking. Don't run both for the same conversions, or Meta receives each one twice. What action_source should a CRM event use? system_generated. The event didn't happen in a browser. Also include custom_data.lead_event_source with your CRM name and custom_data.event_source set to crm, otherwise Meta may accept the event and not use it for lead optimization. Should fbc and fbp be hashed? No. Click and browser identifiers go in plain text. Only personal data like email and phone are hashed with SHA-256.
